title: Demonstrate an understanding of occupational health, safety and environmental legislation relevant to the food or beverage environment

lessons.title: Health and safety law at work
lessons.html:
Health and safety law at work

Food and drink are made in many places on and near farms: pack houses, dairies, cellars, abattoirs, juice plants and bakeries. These workplaces have hazards such as wet floors, sharp knives, hot water, steam, moving machines, chemicals for cleaning and heavy lifting.

The Occupational Health and Safety Act

The main law is the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (the OHS Act). It says that the employer must provide a workplace that is safe and without risk to health, as far as is reasonably practicable. The employer must:

  • find hazards and reduce the risks;
  • give workers information, training and supervision;
  • supply safety equipment (PPE) where it is needed, free of charge;
  • keep machines safe and guarded;
  • appoint health and safety representatives where the law requires it.

Your duties as a worker

The OHS Act also gives duties to employees. You must:

  • take care of your own health and safety and that of others;
  • follow the safety rules and instructions;
  • use the PPE given to you, such as gloves, boots, aprons, hairnets and ear plugs;
  • report any unsafe situation or incident to your supervisor as soon as you can;
  • never interfere with guards or safety devices.

Health and safety representatives and committees

A health and safety representative is a worker chosen to help keep the workplace safe. They inspect the area, talk to workers and report problems to management. In bigger workplaces there is a health and safety committee that meets to discuss problems and plans.

Injuries at work

If a worker is injured or becomes ill because of work, the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act (COIDA) provides for compensation. Always report injuries so they can be recorded.

lessons.title: Food safety and environmental care
lessons.html:
Food safety and environmental care

In a food or beverage workplace you must protect yourself, the food and the environment. Dirty food can make many people sick, so the rules are strict.

Food safety rules

Food businesses must follow food hygiene regulations and the buyer's standards. Many use a system called HACCP, which finds the points where food can become unsafe and controls them. As a worker you help by:

  • washing hands before work, after the toilet, after breaks and after touching rubbish;
  • wearing clean protective clothing, a hairnet and closed shoes;
  • not working with food when you have diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected cut, and telling your supervisor;
  • not eating, smoking or spitting in food areas;
  • keeping cleaning chemicals away from food;
  • reporting pests such as rats, flies and cockroaches.

Environmental law

Food plants use a lot of water and make waste. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 controls water use and pollution of water. The National Environmental Management Act 107 of 1998 (NEMA) says everyone must avoid causing pollution and damage to the environment.

In practice this means:

  • do not wash waste, fat, blood or chemicals into rivers or storm water drains;
  • separate waste: food waste, packaging for recycling, and hazardous waste such as chemical containers;
  • close taps and report leaks to save water;
  • clean up spills quickly, using the right spill kit;
  • switch off machines and lights when not needed.

What never to do

  • Never mix cleaning chemicals; some mixtures give off poisonous gas.
  • Never store chemicals in food or drink bottles.
  • Never hide an accident or a spill.

Key points

  • The OHS Act 85 of 1993 puts duties on both employer and employee.
  • Workers must follow rules, use PPE and report hazards and incidents.
  • Health and safety representatives help keep the workplace safe.
  • Good hygiene protects the food and the people who eat it.
  • Environmental laws such as the National Water Act and NEMA require us to prevent pollution and save resources.

quiz.question: What is the main health and safety law for South African workplaces?

options.text: The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993

quiz.question: Who must supply the PPE that a job needs?
What should a food worker do if they have diarrhoea?

options.text: Tell the supervisor and not work with food

quiz.question: What does a health and safety representative do?

options.text: Inspects the work area and reports problems to management

quiz.question: Where should blood and fat from a food plant NOT go?

options.text: Into a storm water drain or river

quiz.question: Under the OHS Act, workers also have duties, such as following safety rules and reporting hazards.
It is safe to mix different cleaning chemicals to make them stronger.
Which are good hygiene practices in a food area? (select all that apply)

options.text: Washing hands after using the toilet
Smoking only near the packing line
